strengths: The strongest engine contract. Logic is declarative first, with typed expressions checked statically against the model. Errors carry file:line, a hint and did-you-mean, and the error messages have snapshot tests.
Failed calls do not advance the clock. The global lock serializes writes, so ordering is deterministic. A fuzz property test checks that the state hash is unchanged after every failed call.

The grader rules are the best of the three. Every individual check must be false at seed, so noop scores 0 for real. Gates multiply the score, so collateral damage takes it to 0. A gate-coverage lint applies. Mutants are generated by the engine, not written by the LLM.
Seeding by simulation makes every row's state legal by construction (events exist, breaches really happened, timestamps are monotonic).
Reset uses the SQLite backup API. The admin surface runs on a separate port the agent cannot reach. Failed builds go to <out>.failed/.
weaknesses: Timers fire every time the clock moves, and every write moves it by 1s. So the reference's own writes can trigger sla_breach on unrelated tickets. Those engine-made changes trip `unchanged: Ticket except TCK-2207`, and the reference scores 0. The gates cannot tell agent writes from engine writes.

The overreach mutant applies the same action to a sibling row. If that row fails a guard (no_oncall, max_escalation), the call returns 4xx and changes nothing. The mutant's end state then equals the reference's, it scores 1.0, and a correct grader is rejected. The same happens on create-type tasks that have no sibling.

The example grader hard-codes TCK-2207 and AGT-0031, but tickets come from the simulation, and only Customer has an anchor. Any change to the simulation policy or the action set during `update` renumbers the tickets and silently breaks existing tasks. The claim that per-entity RNG streams keep old tasks passing does not hold for simulated entities.
The stage-3 scenarios run before the stage-4 seed exists, and the plan never says what state they run against. The escalate guard needs OnCallShift rows inside the right time window.
A generic simulator for arbitrary workflows written by the LLM has to invent action inputs (agent_id, reason), handle guard failures and pace arrivals. That is a research project inside a 10-day box.

`lookup(...).response_minutes` blows up at runtime when nothing matches, so a missing SlaPolicy combination makes every POST /tickets fail. The type checker has to treat lookup results as Optional and force a default.

The `py:` escape hatch relies on an AST scan plus settrace step limits, which is not a sandbox. getattr chains, generator frames and decimal contexts are all ways out. settrace also slows execution by roughly 10x.
The OpenAPI importer narrows only through `--narrow`. With no flag, a Stripe-sized spec is turned into skeletons that do not fit in context.
Scope is too large for the time box: a type checker, soundness passes, simulation, six verify checks, both importers and update. Nothing says what gets cut.

strengths: The best repair-loop engineering. Fingerprints are sets of (code, path), which catch oscillation. A stall triggers model escalation. A patch that adds errors in untouched paths is reverted automatically. owner_stage drives backtracking through a typed `amend` that writes its reason into the assumptions.
The best OpenAPI ingest. It builds an operation index for large specs, cuts circular refs, computes the transitive schema closure, logs dropped operations and runs a conformance diff afterwards.
The CSV profile is computed in code: FK detection by value overlap, enum candidates, PII flags. The model sees only the profile and samples.
The tasks stage gets a `query_seed` tool, so tasks are built on real seed facts, not invented ones.
It has --resume checkpointing, per-role models, scope shedding limited to optional plan items, and a verify output pasted verbatim into the report.
weaknesses: The decoys are written by the same LLM that writes the grader. Its examples prove nothing. 'Use generic update to force status' is refused by the engine, so that decoy is a noop and trivially scores below 1. An LLM can always write decoys that error out. Decoys measure nothing unless their calls must succeed and their end state must differ from the reference's.

The collateral mutant adds one destructive call on an unrelated row. A DELETE refused by on_delete restrict leaves the end state equal to the reference's, so it scores 1 and verify fails spuriously. A cap of 0.5 instead of 0 also gives a destructive solution half credit.

Stage-3 tests run against a fixture of 5 rows per entity built from defaults. Defaults won't satisfy required refs, state-conditional invariants or time-window rows (on-call shifts). Tests either fail for reasons that have nothing to do with the logic, or pass on the fixture and fail on the real seed.
The seed PRNG is keyed by (world hash, ...). If the world hash covers tasks or logic, any change request reshuffles every row. That contradicts the 'byte-for-byte preserved' seed migration.

Static generators with state-conditional fields can produce states the workflow could never reach: status=escalated with escalation_level=0 and no escalated event. Only the invariants someone thought to declare will catch it.

RFC 6902 patches written by an LLM use array-index JSON pointers. They often fail to apply or hit the wrong element after an earlier insert, which burns repair attempts. Index shifts also change the (code, path) fingerprints, which weakens oscillation detection.
A reference that contains clock moves cannot be repeated by the agent under test, because the agent has no clock endpoint. Such a 'hard' task is unsolvable through the public API.

'Structured output removes YAML errors' assumes a recursive Pydantic schema full of discriminated unions will fit the provider's structured-output and strict-schema limits. It may be rejected or degrade. Also, temperature=0 conflicts with extended thinking on current models.

Scope is the largest of the three: amend and backtracking, impact-analysis dependency graphs, seed migration, a 30-prompt nightly eval at about $8 each, Stripe and GitHub ingest. There are no cut lines.

strengths: The only plan with a credible schedule: an end-to-end slice on day 2, an engine feature freeze, explicit MUST/SHOULD/COULD/WON'T cut lines and a buffer day.
The stress suite includes vague and impossible prompts that must fail honestly. CI replays recorded LLM fixtures.
Graders use `seed.*`/`seed_now` predicates relative to the seed, which survive a seed regeneration better than hard-coded IDs.
The engine generates mutants from the call sequence. The first-page-only and idempotence mutants target real grader weaknesses.
Practical touches: a path allowlist in the edit tool so WorldGen cannot touch engine/, search/replace edits for large files, and a Slack plan with early questions.
weaknesses: The sample grader breaks its own rule. Collateral is an additive check with weight 0.4, and it is true at seed, so noop scores 0.4. A destructive 'escalate all urgent tickets' run scores 0.6 + 0, capped at 0.5. Collateral has to be a gate that multiplies the score to 0, never a weight.

The 'reference executed twice' mutant must score below 1. For idempotent tasks (assign to X, set priority) running twice gives the same end state, so correct graders fail verify. Mutants that fail or have no effect break things here too.

Custom logic is Python by default, and an AST lint is not a sandbox. If ctx keeps a reference to the connection or store (ctx._conn, ctx.__dict__ through getattr), handlers can skip enforcement. Runtime errors only surface through scenario tests the LLM wrote itself.

seed/generator.py is arbitrary LLM code run inside the engine process. Leaks the lint misses include set iteration order over strings (PYTHONHASHSEED), uuid4, os.urandom, date.today() and hash(). The plan also uses one shared RNG, so patching the generator during update shifts every later entity. 'Unchanged entities stay identical' is false.
A Python grader escape hatch means graders the model writes can read anything. That defeats 'graders are declarative and checkable'.

A static reference call list cannot express 'every breached urgent ticket'. The grader text contains a `<target set>` placeholder that is never defined, and the plan never says how the first-page-only mutant is generated from a call list with no loop.
Stage-3 scenario tests have the same problem as A: they come before the seed and have no defined fixture.
Seven days with OpenAPI, CSV and update all treated as MUST or SHOULD is still tight. The engine freeze on D2 will slip once grader and mutant semantics need fixes.

best_ideas_to_keep: From A: declarative state machines, actions and timers with typed expressions checked statically. Make it the only logic path for generated worlds.
From A: noop=0 enforced per check (every positive check must be false at seed). Gates multiply the score.
From A: error JSON with code, path, file:line, hint and did-you-mean, capped and deduplicated, with snapshot tests on error messages.
From A: a failed call rolls back and does not advance the clock. A property test fuzzes calls and asserts the state hash is unchanged.
From A: the admin surface lives on a separate port or an in-process API. Reset uses the SQLite backup API.
From A/C: a gate-coverage lint. Every entity the reference writes must be covered by an unchanged-except gate, or the task declares collateral: allowed with a reason.
From B: repair fingerprints, so a repeated fingerprint switches to a full rewrite with the history attached. A patch that adds errors in untouched paths is auto-reverted. A stall escalates the model.
From B: owner_stage on every error plus a bounded `amend` for upstream fixes, with the reason recorded in the assumptions.

From B: an OpenAPI operation index above a size threshold, a cheap LLM pick capped at about 25 operations when no narrowing flag is given, a transitive schema closure, a dropped-operations log and a conformance diff.
From B: the CSV profile is computed in code, with FK detection by value overlap. The model sees only the profile and samples.
From B: a `query_seed` tool in the tasks stage, plus anchor/needle rows recorded by role.
From C: an end-to-end slice by day 2, cut lines, an engine feature freeze, a stress suite that includes vague and impossible prompts, and recorded-LLM CI fixtures.
From C: grader predicates relative to the seed (seed.*, seed_now) rather than hard-coded IDs.
From C: an edit-tool path allowlist so WorldGen cannot write to engine/.
From all three: the LLM writes a seed spec, not rows. The engine materializes it and the frozen lock file is canonical.
gaps_in_all_plans: Engine changes vs collateral gates. Timers fire as the per-write clock advances, and they change rows the agent never touched. Under 'unchanged except target' gates, the reference then scores 0, or the grader passes only by luck of timing. Every write in the log needs an origin tag (agent call vs timer or cascade). Collateral diffs should count only rows changed by agent-originated effects, or compare against a noop run pushed through the same clock trajectory.

Mutants that fail or have no effect. A mutant whose extra call returns 4xx, or whose end state equals the reference's (idempotent re-run, guard refusal, FK restrict), scores 1.0, and verify falsely rejects a correct grader. Every mutant needs all its calls to return 2xx and an end-state hash that differs from the reference's. Otherwise it is discarded and the engine picks another sibling, and is logged as 'not applicable'.

Clock advances inside references. The agent under test cannot reach the admin clock, so a reference that advances time cannot be repeated through the public API. Time jumps must be part of task `setup` (applied before the agent starts, and before noop too). Only public routes are allowed in references, and a lint must reject any /_admin call.

References cannot loop. Bulk tasks ('every breached urgent ticket') and tasks that need paging can't be written as static call lists, and the 'first page only' mutant has nothing to cut. References need declarative `foreach` over a captured list and a `paginate_all` capture helper.

References that skip discovery. A lint must require that every ID in a reference write comes from a capture or appears literally in the instruction. Otherwise the reference passes using knowledge the agent doesn't have, and the task's difficulty is fake.

Alternative valid solutions. No plan checks that a different correct path also scores 1, for example assign then escalate vs escalate directly, or paging with a different sort. At least one engine-generated variant of the reference should run (reordered independent writes, a different list sort or page size) and must still score 1.

Logic tests have no data. Stage 3 runs before seed in A and C, and B's fixture built from defaults is invalid. Scenarios should carry inline `given:` rows, which the engine validates under the full constraints.

Seed IDs are unstable across `update`. Hard-coded task IDs (A), RNG keyed by world hash (B) and one shared RNG (C) all break existing tasks after a change request. Each entity needs its own hashlib-derived RNG stream keyed by rng_seed and entity name. The lock file is canonical and old rows are never regenerated. New fields are backfilled from separate streams.

Iteration can quietly weaken old graders. Gates written as explicit entity lists (A) don't cover entities added later, such as Refund rows created by a confused agent. Gates should default to 'whole world unchanged except ...' so new entities are covered automatically. A new timer or workflow can also change existing rows at clock ticks, which needs a regression check on every old task's noop, reference and mutant results.

Hidden determinism leaks: float money (use integer minor units or Decimal stored as TEXT), Faker version drift (pin it, and treat the lock as canonical), Python hash() on strings, SQLite LIKE/NOCASE handling only ASCII, inconsistent datetime formats and timezones in canonical JSON, and cursor encoding that depends on dict order.

Structured-output limits. Recursive Pydantic schemas with many discriminated unions may exceed what the provider's strict tool schema accepts. Keep expressions as strings, keep the schema shallow and keyed by name, and validate in the engine rather than relying on decoding.
Repair edits keyed by array index. Model, route and action collections should be maps keyed by name, not lists. Then patches and search/replace target stable keys, and fingerprints don't shift.

Fidelity knobs for OpenAPI input. Stripe-style `starting_after`/`has_more`, offset/limit, nested routes scoped to a parent (/customers/{id}/sources) and idempotency keys need configurable pagination parameter names and parent-scoped CRUD in the engine. Otherwise the 'follows the spec' requirement fails even when ingest works.
Verify throughput during the live run. Spinning up uvicorn ports for each mutant and repair is slow and flaky. Verify should drive the same ASGI app in-process with a test client.

Realistic text. Faker gives lorem-style subjects. A cheap model should produce domain value pools once, cached into the world with seeded sampling. Without that, 'plausible values' fails even when the structure is perfect.

Read-and-report tasks. None of the plans can grade 'how many tickets breached?' without an answer channel. Either add POST /_task/answer, graded by expressions, or declare such tasks out of scope in the design doc.
recommended_decisions: Generated worlds use only declarative logic: state machines, guards, effects and timers. If the Python escape hatch is kept at all, it is for the hand-built world only, behind a ctx proxy that holds no connection reference. Reason: an AST lint is not a sandbox, and runtime-only failures make the repair loop much worse.

Collateral is always a multiplicative gate that takes the score to 0, and it defaults to 'entire world unchanged except declared patterns'. Reason: C's additive weight gives noop 0.4 and a destructive solution 0.5, and listing entities by hand misses entities added later.
Diffs are attributed by origin: writes are tagged agent-call vs timer/cascade, and gates only examine changes the agent caused. Reason: otherwise background timers make reference solutions fail.

Mutants are generated only by the engine (prefix, wrong-target sibling, overbroad foreach, double-run). Each is used only if all its calls return 2xx and its end-state hash differs from the reference's. Decoys written by the LLM are dropped. Reason: the model grading its own grader is self-grading in disguise.

Clock advances belong in task `setup`, never in references. References may call only public routes, and every ID they write must come from a capture or the instruction. Reason: a task the agent cannot solve through the API is not a task.

References are declarative call lists with `capture`, `foreach` and `paginate_all`. Reason: bulk and paging tasks, the 'hard' tier, can't be written otherwise, and code references reopen the sandbox problem.

Seed for v1 uses static, state-conditional generators. Each state machine must declare invariants per state, the engine checks them, and child event rows are auto-derived from the state. A's full simulation is SHOULD-tier. Reason: a generic simulator over LLM-written workflows needs action-input synthesis and is the largest schedule risk.

Seed RNG is one stream per entity, derived with hashlib from (rng_seed, entity). The lock file is canonical, and update never regenerates existing rows. Reason: it is the only way existing tasks survive change requests.
Logic scenarios carry inline `given:` fixture rows that the engine validates. Reason: it removes the stage-3/stage-4 ordering hole without depending on the seed.

Model, route, action and task collections are YAML maps keyed by name. Repairs are keyed object replacements or search/replace, not RFC 6902 index patches. Reason: stable edit targets and stable fingerprints.

Use B's repair controls (fingerprint oscillation, auto-revert on regression, stall escalation, a bounded amend budget) inside C's per-stage attempt caps plus global USD and wall-clock caps. Reason: convergence control without burning the budget.

Follow C's schedule shape: an end-to-end slice on day 2 with an engine freeze after day 3. Importers and update are SHOULD-tier, and the stress suite has 12-15 prompts, not 30 nightly. Reason: the live run rewards a working, hardened pipeline over breadth.
Verify runs in-process against the ASGI app with a test client, and resets between runs use the SQLite backup API. Reason: speed and no port flakiness during repair loops.

Money is stored as integer minor units. Canonical JSON has sorted keys, RFC 3339 UTC timestamps and id-tiebroken ordering. A CI test runs everything twice and compares hashes. Reason: it closes the common determinism leaks.

Expressions are stored as strings in the schema, the tool input schema stays shallow, and the engine stays the validator. Reason: deep recursive and union-heavy schemas risk hitting structured-output limits.

OpenAPI input with no narrowing flag gets B's operation index plus a cheap LLM pick capped at about 25 operations, and the dropped operations are logged in the report. Reason: large specs must never reach the prompt raw.
